questions.question: According to the CAP theorem, during a network partition, a distributed system must choose between:

options.text: Consistency and Latency
Availability and Throughput
Consistency and Availability
Partition tolerance and Durability

questions.explanation: CAP states that during a partition (P), you cannot have both Consistency (C) and Availability (A). You must choose to either return potentially stale data (AP) or reject requests until consistency is restored (CP). Eric Brewer formalized this in 2000, and Gilbert & Lynch proved it in 2002. The key insight: partitions are inevitable in distributed systems (networks fail), so the real choice is between C and A when partitions occur. During normal operation, you can have both.

questions.question: A banking system requires that account balances are always accurate, even if it means rejecting transactions during network issues. Which CAP classification best describes this system?

options.text: AP (Availability + Partition tolerance) with eventual consistency
CP (Consistency + Partition tolerance) with reduced availability
CA (Consistency + Availability) with partition avoidance
Tunable consistency based on transaction amount

questions.explanation: The system prioritizes consistency over availability. This is a CP system. CA is impossible in distributed systems because partitions are inevitable. Traditional banks use CP systems for core banking. An ATM that cannot reach the network will decline transactions rather than risk overdrafts. The regulatory requirement for accurate financial records makes CP the only viable choice for banking core systems.

questions.question: Which statement about the CAP theorem is FALSE?

options.text: The tradeoff between C and A only applies during network partitions
A system must permanently sacrifice one of the three properties at design time
Most distributed systems are partition-tolerant by necessity
The choice between C and A can be made differently for different operations

questions.explanation: CAP tradeoffs only apply during partitions. When the network is healthy, a system can provide both consistency and availability. The theorem does not require permanently sacrificing one property. Modern systems like CockroachDB and Spanner provide strong consistency AND high availability during normal operation, only sacrificing availability in the minority partition during network splits.

questions.question: A social media platform shows slightly outdated follower counts but never goes offline. Which CAP properties does it prioritize?

options.text: Consistency and Availability (CA)
Consistency and Partition tolerance (CP)
Availability and Partition tolerance (AP)
Strong consistency with async replication

questions.explanation: The system accepts stale data (relaxed consistency) to remain available during partitions. This is an AP system. Twitter, Instagram, and Facebook all use AP designs for non-critical data like follower counts and likes. Users tolerate seeing approximate numbers but will not tolerate the app being unavailable. For critical features like direct messages, these same platforms often use CP subsystems.

questions.question: Why is a CA (Consistency + Availability without Partition tolerance) system impractical for distributed systems?

options.text: Network partitions are inevitable in any distributed system
CA systems require specialized hardware that is prohibitively expensive
The CAP theorem mathematically proves CA is impossible
CA systems cannot scale beyond a single data center

questions.explanation: Network partitions (hardware failures, network issues, cable cuts, BGP misconfigurations) are unavoidable in distributed systems. A CA system would fail entirely during partitions. Google Spanner paper notes they experience network partitions regularly despite their private network. Practical distributed systems must be partition-tolerant, leaving the C vs A choice. Single-node databases are technically CA but are not distributed systems.

questions.question: Which databases are typically classified as CP systems? (Choose all that apply)

options.text: MongoDB with majority write concern and read concern
Apache Cassandra with consistency level ONE
Google Cloud Spanner
Amazon DynamoDB with eventual consistency reads

questions.explanation: MongoDB with majority write/read concern and Spanner prioritize consistency, potentially rejecting operations during partitions when quorum cannot be reached. Cassandra with CL=ONE and DynamoDB with eventual reads are AP. The key insight: many databases are configurable. Cassandra with CL=QUORUM behaves more like CP; DynamoDB with strongly consistent reads behaves more like CP. The CAP classification depends on configuration, not just the database product.

questions.question: A distributed database uses quorum reads and writes (majority of replicas). During a partition that isolates the minority of nodes, what happens?

options.text: The minority partition continues serving reads and writes normally
The minority partition becomes unavailable for writes but may serve stale reads
Both partitions continue operating independently, causing split-brain
The entire system shuts down until the partition heals

questions.explanation: Quorum systems require majority agreement for writes. The minority partition cannot achieve write quorum, so it rejects writes to maintain consistency. Depending on configuration, it might serve stale reads or reject all operations. The majority partition continues operating normally. This is CP behavior. etcd, Consul, and ZooKeeper all exhibit this behavior. The minority partition is available in the sense of responding, but unavailable for making progress.

questions.question: A common misconception is that CAP means you must permanently choose two of three properties. What does CAP actually mean?

options.text: You must choose two properties at system design time and cannot change
During partitions, you choose C or A; during normal operation, you can have both
You can have all three properties but with degraded performance
The choice applies only to write operations, not reads

questions.explanation: CAP tradeoffs apply during partitions only. Systems can provide both consistency and availability during normal operation. The choice between C and A is made when partitions occur, and can even vary per operation or data type. Spanner provides strong consistency AND five-nines availability during normal operation. It only sacrifices availability in minority partitions during network splits.

questions.question: A system architect wants to build a globally distributed database that is always consistent and always available. What should you tell them?

options.text: Use synchronous replication across all regions with consensus protocols
This is impossible according to CAP theorem during network partitions
Use a consensus algorithm like Paxos or Raft to achieve both
Deploy in a single region with multiple availability zones

questions.explanation: CAP proves this is impossible during partitions. Synchronous replication and consensus algorithms help with consistency but sacrifice availability during partitions. If a region is unreachable, writes to that region data block or fail. Single region avoids the distributed system context but does not provide global distribution. Google Spanner comes closest by using GPS-synchronized clocks, but even Spanner sacrifices availability in minority partitions.

questions.question: Which strategy allows a system to provide different CAP tradeoffs for different types of data?

options.text: Using a single database with configurable consistency levels per query
Polyglot persistence with different databases for different data types
Tunable consistency levels per operation or table
All of the above are valid approaches

questions.explanation: All approaches work: single DBs with configurable consistency (Cassandra consistency levels, DynamoDB read consistency), multiple specialized databases (polyglot persistence), or per-operation tuning. Critical data like financial transactions can use CP settings while less critical data like view counts uses AP settings. Netflix uses this pattern: user credentials in CP storage, viewing history in AP storage. CAP tradeoffs should be made per-data-type based on business requirements.

questions.question: During a network partition, a CP system receives a write request for data whose replicas are split across both partitions. What is the expected behavior?

options.text: Accept the write and synchronize when the partition heals
Reject the write or block until the partition heals
Write to the local partition only and mark as tentative
Redirect the request to whichever partition has more replicas

questions.explanation: CP systems prioritize consistency. They will not accept writes that cannot be consistently replicated to a quorum. The system either rejects the request with an error or blocks until it can guarantee consistency across sufficient replicas. This is exactly what happens with etcd, ZooKeeper, and Consul during partitions. The minority partition becomes read-only or fully unavailable to prevent split-brain.

questions.question: Which real-world scenario best illustrates the practical implications of the CAP tradeoff?

options.text: Choosing between SQL and NoSQL databases for a new project
An ATM deciding whether to allow withdrawals during network outage
Selecting between vertical and horizontal scaling strategies
Deciding between synchronous and asynchronous API designs

questions.explanation: ATM during network outage perfectly illustrates CAP: allow withdrawal (AP, available but potentially inconsistent with actual balance, risking overdraft) or decline (CP, consistent but unavailable, frustrating customer). Banks historically chose CP (decline), but some now allow small offline withdrawals (AP for small amounts, CP for large). This real-world example shows CAP is not just theoretical. It is a business decision with real consequences.
